source_defaults.notes: Original WTTW candidate statement and questionnaire, explicitly identified in the retained text as the March 2020 primary guide. Exact original publication and pre-primary version are unverified; the 2026 retrieval is not backdated. Wayback availability found no pre-primary version for these exact URLs. Claims are the candidates' statements, not independent factual verification.

historical_cycle_evidence.exact_quote: You have reached the 2020 Primary Election (March 2020) Voter Guide.

statements.claim: Names Medicare for All as a human right within a linked economic-equality agenda.
Supports a Green New Deal; this answer does not supply every implementation detail.

statements.quote: Economic inequality is the most pressing issue
statements.claim: Presents economic inequality as the root linking housing, health, violence, education and environmental problems.

statements.quote: utilize the seat as a vehicle
statements.claim: Frames the congressional seat as a vehicle for coalition building and collective working-class representation rather than individual advancement.
Supports a federal jobs guarantee as part of an interconnected economic program.
Names a Homes Guarantee; this passage alone does not specify its complete financing or delivery design.

statements.quote: making health care a right with Medicare-for-All
statements.claim: Explicitly supports Medicare for All, not merely defending the ACA.

statements.quote: addressing global climate change with a Green New Deal
statements.claim: Explicitly supports a Green New Deal.
Answers the most-pressing-issue question by emphasizing economic and social inequality and naming healthcare, climate, college, childcare and wage remedies.
Campaigns on an established progressive record and repeated electoral support as evidence of representation.
Supports a $15 minimum wage as an inequality-reduction measure.

statements.quote: a single-payer Medicare for All system
statements.claim: Supports single-payer Medicare for All and describes previous organizing for it.

statements.quote: a core component of my fight for social justice
statements.claim: Centers gun-violence prevention as a public-health and social-justice priority; the complete answer also identifies healthcare and criminal-justice reform.

statements.quote: will not accept a single penny from corporations
statements.claim: Says the campaign rejects corporate funding. This is a stated campaign commitment, not an independent finance audit.

statements.quote: add a public health insurance option
statements.claim: Proposes improving the ACA with a public option alongside private plans and additional drug-price measures.

statements.quote: The first priority will be to reduce hunger
statements.claim: Names hunger reduction as the office's first priority, including more federal funding, increased SNAP benefits and food access. In a separate answer she calls healthcare constituents' most pressing issue.

statements.quote: from the courthouse into the halls of Congress
statements.claim: Presents courtroom and lobbying achievements as a practical human-rights record to carry into Congress.

comparisons.analysis: Clark and incumbent Davis both explicitly support Medicare for All. Their challenger/incumbent roles do not establish a single-payer versus ACA-only divide.

Both support single-payer Medicare for All; Collins also describes organizing for that proposal. The retained registry groups Clark as endorsed for this race, without projecting Collins's later endorsement history backward.

Clark proposes Medicare for All while Schanbacher proposes an ACA public option with private plans. This compares stated insurance architectures; the answer is not coded as an explicit categorical rejection of every single-payer proposal.
Both explicitly name support for a Green New Deal. The statements establish shared support for the named proposal, not identical detailed implementation plans.
Both answer the pressing-issue question through economic inequality and a linked set of reforms. Their different political biographies should not erase this common campaign frame.

Clark emphasizes movement-building and collective working-class power; Davis emphasizes his progressive record and constituent mandate. This is a contrast in self-presentation, not proof that one lacks progressive policies.

Clark organizes his answer around economic inequality as a root cause; Collins foregrounds gun violence, healthcare and criminal justice. The topics overlap and are not mutually exclusive commitments.

Clark frames economic inequality as the connecting root cause; Schanbacher names hunger reduction as an initial office priority and healthcare as constituents' pressing issue. Neither statement proves indifference to the other's concern.
Clark emphasizes organizing collective working-class power; Schanbacher emphasizes transferring her human-rights litigation and lobbying experience into legislative results.
